q-161220.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225003/assets/e8708a16a0f6db347acf2c1a82a602d2fa8ce60d4bb8369f1414eca3465e4e71.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
q-161220.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225003/assets/8ed6ffdeab54bc6888d245ef4f1c050c31e010c67dfa93aea365fc6cb523e382.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-4⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =2x+y-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2x+y-4\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x+y-4\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x+y-4\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[{x}^{2}+xy-4x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}y-3\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-3y]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-(2x+y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-(2x+y)\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}2x+y\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x+y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{[{x}^{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}1+y\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{15}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}+(-\frac{15}{2}) \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨4{x}^{3}+3{y}^{2}+2z,\,0,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $x$-component of $F=⟨4{x}^{3}+3{y}^{2}+2z,\,0,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $x$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the front and back sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225003/assets/4fd228a9bf0a2d8382139d3f804ee7c9b3fd8721c8ad079de43e61b9e8947240.png)

  

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=1$ for $0\le y\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨4{x}^{3}+3{y}^{2}+2z,\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨4+3{y}^{2}+2z,\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =4+3{y}^{2}+2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}4+3{y}^{2}+2z\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}4+3{y}^{2}+2z\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}4+3{y}^{2}+2z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[(4+2z)y+{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4+2z+1\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2z+5\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[{z}^{2}+5z]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =9+15 \\  & =24\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for $0\le y\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨4{x}^{3}+3{y}^{2}+2z,\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨3{y}^{2}+2z,\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =-(3{y}^{2}+2z).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-(3{y}^{2}+2z)\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}3{y}^{2}+2z\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}3{y}^{2}+2z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{[{y}^{3}+2yz]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}1+2z\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{[z+{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-(3+9) \\  & =-12\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =24+(-12) \\  & =12.\end{aligned}

q-161219.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=4$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}x{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4x]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+8\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}+8y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{26}{3}.\end{aligned}

$$

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=2$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,3{x}^{2}y+2z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,6{x}^{2}+2z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =6{x}^{2}+2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}6{x}^{2}+2z\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}6{x}^{2}+2z\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}6{x}^{2}+2z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2{x}^{3}+2xz]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}16+4z\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[16z+2{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =18\end{aligned}

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$

$$

q-161162.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225003/assets/8fa71e16d84eb92506e9b10269182f907cb4f2437d0a9bdd3822da48c4cbba4a.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+yz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+2y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =2x+2y.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}{S}_{1} & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2x+2y\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x+2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x+2y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}+2xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+2y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[y+{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+yz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-2x.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}{S}_{2} & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-2x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}-2x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-1\cdot {[{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-1\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =2+(-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field F(x,y,z)=⟨0,0,2x+yz⟩ and the surface S defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of F through S.

a
2
b
4
c
1
d
0
e
3

Correct
EXPLANATION

If S is an oriented surface with unit normal vector n, and F is continuous vector field, then the flux of F across S measured with respect to n is given by

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS.

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of F across S1 as follows: ∬S1F⋅dS1=∬S1F⋅n1dS=∬S12x+2ydS=∬D2x+2ydA=∫01∫012x+2ydxdy=∫01[x2+2xy]x=0x=1dy=∫011+2ydy=[y+y2]01=2.

  • Let S2 denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have z=0 for 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤1. The outward-pointing unit normal vector to S2 is n2=⟨0,0,−1⟩. Using the fact that z=0 on S2, we have F⋅n2=⟨0,0,2x+yz⟩⋅⟨0,0,−1⟩=⟨0,0,2x⟩⋅⟨0,0,−1⟩=−2x. Finally,

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬S1F⋅ndS+∬S2F⋅ndS=2+(−1)=1.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225003/assets/dedd58b5eeeba8b2874c740543132026f95157597dd12ad31fbaa476a3d77c2e.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,{y}^{2}(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}),\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $4$ whose base is a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
q-162547.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,{y}^{2}(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}),\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the left and right sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225003/assets/9ffcdd701a8ac6b12cd62773e1cabfd2ce95f9a809e18d087c4bf4f4a22eadb5.png)

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=4$ for ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 9.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=4$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,{y}^{2}(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}),\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,({4}^{2})(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}),\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,16(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}),\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =16(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}16(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =16{∬}_{D}(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,z)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}16{∬}_{D}(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =16{∬}_{D}(6-{r}^{2})\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r(6-{r}^{2})\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}(6r-{r}^{3})\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}(6r-{r}^{3})\,\text{d}r \\  & =16\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[3{r}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =32\pi (27-\frac{81}{4}) \\  & =32\pi (\frac{27}{4}) \\  & =216\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 9.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(x,0,z)=⟨0,\,{0}^{2}(6-{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}),\,0⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =216\pi +0 \\  & =216\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
